title: Contracts that may be PPPs: DBFOM, concessions and variations
objectives: Explain how a DBOM contract works and why it is an infrastructure PPP but not a private finance PPP.
Describe a DBFOM contract and when it is a true private finance PPP.
Compare user-pays PPPs (concessions) with government-pays PPPs (PFI, availability payments).
Explain the viability gap, co-financing and hybrid schemes.
Distinguish joint ventures, institutional PPPs and public-public partnerships, and say which the Guide treats as PPPs.

sections.heading: 1. DBOM: bundled, but publicly financed
sections.body:
In the last lesson we saw contracts that are **not** PPPs: B, DB and DBF. Now we move to contracts that **may** be PPPs.

The first is **DBOM (Design, Build, Operate and Maintain)**. The government still **finances the works from its budget**, as in conventional procurement. But the same contractor also carries out **future operations and maintenance**. If the contractor does not operate the asset, the contract is usually called **DBM**.

**How it works (Figure 1.4):**

- Construction is **paid directly as work progresses**.
- Maintenance is **pre-contracted** at a **pre-agreed price**. The **O&M price** is closely tied to the **performance of the O&M work** and paid in a **separate stream**.
- The contractor delivers the asset at completion and then provides maintenance (or O&M).

**The limits of DBOM:**

- There may still be an incentive to **reduce construction quality** to save costs, so quality must be carefully controlled.
- The risk of unexpected maintenance costs can be transferred only **in a limited way**, usually through **liquidated damages** (pre-agreed amounts payable for a failure).
- The **main part of maintenance risk**, which depends on good design and construction, usually **stays with the government**.

Even so, if maintenance risk is transferred together with construction risk, a DBOM **may be close to the PPP concept** in scope and efficiency, even though there is **no capital at risk**. For this reason **many countries regard DBOM as a type of PPP**. The Guide calls DBOM an **infrastructure PPP without private finance**. It is **not a private finance PPP**. Only DBOM and DBFOM-type contracts (such as BOT) bundle **long-term maintenance** with construction, and they are usually the only forms where pay is based on the **performance of the asset**.

**Why choose DBOM?** The government may prefer it when the benefit of **integrated management** outweighs the efficiency lost by giving up a **separate competition for the future O&M contract**. This often happens when the project and financial context **do not justify a private finance PPP**.

sections.heading: 2. DBFOM: the typical private finance PPP
sections.body:
In a **DBFOM (Design, Build, Finance, Operate and Maintain)** contract, the contractor develops the infrastructure with **its own funds and funds from lenders, at its own risk**. It provides **all or most of the financing**. It also manages the **asset's life cycle**, taking **life-cycle cost risk**, as well as current maintenance and operations. The private partner usually creates an **SPV** to do this. When operations are not included, the contract is often called **DBFM**.

DBFOM and DBFM, together with equivalent terms such as **BOT** (Build-Operate-Transfer), **BOOT** (Build-Own-Operate-Transfer) and **BTO** (Build-Transfer-Operate), are **the only contract type, in terms of scope, that can meet all the conditions of a private finance PPP**.

But the name alone is not enough. Whether a DBFOM is a **true** private finance PPP depends on:

- how **effective the risk transfer** is; and
- how **closely revenue is linked to performance**.

Some DBFOMs are really a **DBOM with private money**, where investors take **no material risk**. In that case the project gives a **value for money (VfM)** result similar to a DBOM, not to a real DBFOM. **Value for money (VfM)**, in the PPP context, means the benefits compared with the costs of using a PPP instead of other procurement options.

DBFOM contracts come in two main types, depending on who pays:

| | User-pays DBFOM | Government-pays DBFOM |
|---|---|---|
| Main revenue | Charges to users (tolls, tariffs, fares) | Payments from the authority's budget |
| Paid for | Use of the asset | Availability and quality (or volume) |
| Other names | **Concession** | **PFI**, availability payment PPP |

The next sections look at each type.

sections.heading: 3. User-pays PPPs (concessions)
sections.body:
When an authority decides to **charge users** for infrastructure, it can use that revenue in several ways. It can go to the **general budget**, to a **sector fund**, or be **earmarked** for the system that generates it. The revenue from a **new** asset can also be earmarked to that specific project and **assigned to an SPV** created by the private partner.

The Guide defines a **user-pays PPP** as a **contractual assignment**, by a public administration to a private party, of the **future revenues from public use** of the infrastructure, used to fund the procurement of the infrastructure and related services. These are also known as **concession schemes**, especially in **civil code countries**.

**Key features:**

- The scope is **DBFOM in an integrated manner**, and the financing is **private**. It is typically treated as private finance under national accounting standards.
- All or most revenue comes from the **right to commercialise the use of the asset**, meaning from users.
- The private partner **recovers its investment** through user payments. It uses them to **repay debt** and pay **returns to investors** (dividends or repayment of shareholder loans).
- The private partner is the **economic owner** of the asset during the contract. It must **maintain and renew** the asset **at its own expense and risk**, with no right to claim from the public party, except where a proper risk allocation says otherwise.
- If revenues **exceed** what is needed for a minimum return, the contract may include **revenue sharing**, meaning a payment from the private party to the authority.

The main contract relationships (Figure 1.5) are: the **authority grants the right to charge users**, and the private partner provides the **bundled DBFOM service**. The private partner is financed by **equity investors** and **lenders**. It **subcontracts** the construction (often to an **EPC contractor**) and the O&M. **Users pay charges** to the private partner. At the end, the asset is **handed back** to the authority.

sections.heading: 4. When user revenue is not enough: viability gap, co-financing and hybrids
sections.body:
A concession needs revenue that is **higher than construction and O&M costs**. The surplus repays the financing and gives investors a return.

Sometimes revenues are **not enough** to cover the partner's financial obligations and a return on equity. The Guide calls this a **financial or commercial viability gap**. If the project still brings enough **economic and social benefits**, the government may decide to **fill the gap**. It can do this through:

- **grants**, known as **co-financing**; or
- **complementary budget payments linked to performance**.

Both are forms of **viability gap funding**.

**Which sectors?** According to the Guide:

- **Roads, airports and ports**, and some **telecom and water** projects, often have user revenue large enough to fund most or all of the project.
- **Rail** almost never covers its costs from users, because of very high capital needs and **socially subsidised fares**. Co-financing and **hybrid payment regimes**, which mix user charges with availability or service payments, are standard.

Other hybrid structures use **capital subsidies** or viability gap financing to **buy down capital costs**. Co-financing can also be used when a project is already viable, for other reasons.

**Mixed-equity companies and joint ventures.** A further variation is where the **government takes equity** in the project company. Names vary: **mixed equity companies** (*empresas mixtas* in Spanish-speaking countries), **joint ventures**, or **institutionalised PPPs** (the EU Commission's term). The Guide uses these as synonyms for structures where the government:

- holds a **material equity stake**;
- has **seats and voting rights** on the SPV board in line with its shares; and
- takes an **active part in management**, for example by appointing senior staff.

A simple **minority stake** with only normal shareholder rights is **not usually** called a joint venture. The line between the two can be very subtle.

sections.heading: 5. Government-pays PPPs (PFI)
sections.body:
Sometimes user revenue is not an option. There may be **no users to charge**. Revenue may be **too small** compared with capital needs, which is typical of rail. Or the government may want the asset to be **free to users**, as with non-toll roads. In these cases the government can still ask a contractor to:

- take on the **full life cycle** of the asset, from construction to renewal;
- **finance** the works with its own funds;
- **maintain and/or operate** the asset to set **service levels**; and
- be paid for **both construction and O&M only as long as, and to the extent that, the asset is available** at the required quality.

This is a **government-pays PPP**, also called a **PFI (Private Finance Initiative)**, the UK name. The revenue comes from **providing a service to the grantor**, which is making the asset available for use. Sometimes the government is **not the user** (a toll-free road). Sometimes the asset is **used by the government** or public staff, such as a **hospital, prison, court or school**.

Government-pays PPPs **may also include user or commercial revenue**. If that revenue is **not the majority**, the contract is still a government-pays PPP. The **co-financing** and **joint venture** variations also apply, although joint ventures are **rarer** in government-pays schemes.

**A special case: tolls kept by the government.** Users may pay a toll, but the toll revenue is **intentionally left out** of the private partner's income. In the **I-595** road project in Florida (2008), the private partner financed most of a road project of about **$1.6 billion** and received **availability payments** once the road opened. The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) also gave **$685 million in deferred grants**. FDOT **kept the toll revenue**, and its risk, and used it to offset the availability payments. This gave FDOT flexibility to use **dynamic tolling to manage congestion**. It also avoided a conflict with a private partner that would want to **maximise revenue**. The grants also let FDOT use part of its budget in the early years and so lower its yearly availability payments.

sections.heading: 6. Public-public partnerships and institutional PPPs
sections.body:
Governments can also create their own companies, **State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs)**, to build, finance and manage infrastructure. They are usually funded by revenue from the asset, such as tolls, transit fares or water tariffs.

When a **public corporation** develops an asset under a DBFOM-style contract from **the government that owns it**, the arrangement can copy much of a real PPP's structure. It may be called a **“public-public partnership”**. **The Guide does not regard these as PPPs.**

- Often there is **no contract in the strict sense**, only a general **authorisation** and assignment of economic rights to the SOE.
- Even with a strict contract and **project finance** techniques, there are **reasonable doubts that any real risk is transferred** to the private sector of the economy.

An example is the EBRD model for urban transport in some European countries. The authority signs a **public service contract** with its own public operator, with payments partly linked to performance. It also signs a **Municipal Support Agreement (MSA)** with the **EBRD**.

**Institutional PPPs** are different. Here a DBFOM contract goes to a project company **jointly owned by public and private partners**, but the **government controls** it, usually by holding **most of the shares**. The Guide treats an institutional PPP as a **true private finance PPP only when**:

- the private sector is a **significant equity investor**, with a significant share of the equity;
- the private partner **assumes project risks** and takes a significant part in management or operations; and
- the **debt is at risk of performance**.

**Madrid Calle 30 example.** Madrid's M-30 ring road project cost about **€4.5 billion**. It was a **35-year DBFOM with availability payments**. The city council held **80%** of the joint venture company and the private partner **20%**. The private partner was chosen by **public tender** and also ran O&M under a back-to-back subcontract. The project aimed to stay **off the city's balance sheet**. But mainly because of **insufficient risk transfer** in Eurostat's view, it was recorded as **public debt**. Even so, the structure gave the private operators good incentives, and the service is well regarded.

The Guide's tender and contract management guidance focuses on **conventional PPPs**, which are privately owned or controlled, possibly with a **minority** public stake.

example.title: Classifying three contracts for the Lakeside Metro region
example.body:
Imagine the fictional Lakeside Transport Authority has three projects.

**Project 1: Ring road.** A private SPV designs, builds, finances, operates and maintains a new toll road for 30 years. It collects the tolls and uses them to repay its lenders and pay its investors. This is a **user-pays DBFOM, a concession**, and a private finance PPP.

**Project 2: Light rail line.** Fares will cover only about a quarter of the costs, because fares are kept low for social reasons. The authority pays a construction **grant** of 30% of capital costs. The SPV collects the fares, and the authority also pays it **availability payments**, with deductions for missed services. This is a **co-financed, hybrid PPP** that fills a **viability gap**. It remains a private finance PPP as long as significant private finance stays at risk.

**Project 3: Depot upgrade.** The authority's own wholly owned transport company signs a 20-year agreement to upgrade and maintain the depot, funded by a loan against its fare income. The structure looks like a PPP, but it is a **public-public partnership**. There is no real transfer of risk to the private sector, so the Guide does **not** treat it as a PPP.

If, instead, a private investor held 49% of the depot company, took real project risk, ran the maintenance, and the debt depended on performance, it could be an **institutional PPP** that counts as a true private finance PPP.

examTraps.trap: Calling DBOM a private finance PPP.
examTraps.fix: DBOM bundles construction and O&M, but the government pays for the works from its budget. It is an infrastructure PPP with no private finance, so it is not a private finance PPP.

examTraps.trap: Assuming every contract labelled DBFOM is a true private finance PPP.
examTraps.fix: It is a true private finance PPP only if investors take material risk and revenue is linked to performance. Otherwise it gives VfM similar to a DBOM.

examTraps.trap: Thinking a toll road must be a user-pays PPP.
examTraps.fix: If the government keeps the tolls and pays the partner availability payments, as in I-595, it is a government-pays PPP. Look at who receives the revenue and who carries demand risk.

examTraps.trap: Confusing public-public partnerships with institutional PPPs.
examTraps.fix: A public-public partnership is 100% public and is not a PPP. An institutional PPP is publicly controlled, with private equity. It counts as a true PPP only if private equity and risk are significant.

examTraps.trap: Believing any public shareholding makes the project a joint venture.
examTraps.fix: A joint venture needs a material public stake, board voting rights and active management. A simple minority stake with normal shareholder rights is usually not called a JV.

keyTerms.meaning: Design, Build, Operate and Maintain: a bundled contract paid from the public budget; an infrastructure PPP without private finance (DBM if there are no operations).
Design, Build, Finance, Operate and Maintain: the private partner finances at its own risk and manages the asset life cycle; the typical private finance PPP (DBFM without operations).
A contractual assignment to a private party of future user revenues from a public asset, used to fund its development and management.
A DBFOM where the partner is paid by the authority, usually through availability payments linked to availability and quality.
The shortfall when user revenues cannot cover the partner's financial obligations and a return on equity.
Public funding, usually grants, that pays part of the capital cost of a PPP asset.
A PPP whose payment regime mixes user charges with availability or service payments, or that uses public or concessional funds (such as capital subsidies) to reach viability.
A project company in which the government holds material equity, votes on the board and takes part in management.
A PPP in which the government controls the project company, usually with majority shares.
A DBFOM-like arrangement with a company wholly owned by the procuring government; not a PPP in the Guide.

summary: DBOM bundles design, build, operation and maintenance but is paid from the budget; it is an infrastructure PPP, not a private finance PPP.
DBFOM (and DBFM, BOT, BOOT, BTO) is the only contract scope that can meet all conditions of a private finance PPP.
A DBFOM is a true private finance PPP only with material risk transfer to investors and revenue linked to performance.
User-pays PPPs (concessions) earn revenue from users; the partner is the economic owner and bears maintenance and renewal risk.
A viability gap can be filled by grants (co-financing) or performance-linked budget payments; rail usually needs hybrid schemes.
Government-pays PPPs (PFI) pay the partner for availability and quality, even when the government collects tolls itself (I-595).
Public-public partnerships are not PPPs; institutional PPPs count only with significant private equity and risk.

slides.title: DBOM: bundled but publicly paid
points: Same contractor designs, builds, operates, maintains
Works paid from the budget as they progress
O&M paid separately, linked to performance
Infrastructure PPP, but no private finance
slides.narration: Welcome back. Today we look at contracts that may be PPPs, starting with DBOM. In a DBOM, one contractor designs, builds, operates and maintains the asset. That bundling is a big step forward from design-build. But the government still pays for the construction from its budget as the work progresses, and pays for operations and maintenance in a separate stream. So there is no private capital at risk. Many countries call DBOM a PPP, and the Guide calls it an infrastructure PPP. But it is not a private finance PPP. Remember that difference.

slides.title: DBFOM: the typical private finance PPP
points: Private partner finances at its own risk
Manages the whole asset life cycle
Also called DBFM, BOT, BOOT, BTO
Only a true PPP with real risk transfer
slides.narration: Now DBFOM: design, build, finance, operate and maintain. Here the private partner, usually through an SPV, raises the money from its investors and lenders, at its own risk. It also looks after the asset for its whole life, including renewals. When there are no operations, we say DBFM. Names like BOT and BOOT describe the same scope. This is the only scope that can meet every condition of a private finance PPP. But watch out. If the investors carry no real risk, a DBFOM is really a DBOM with private money, and gives similar value for money.

slides.title: User-pays: the concession
points: Partner earns revenue from users
Revenue repays debt and rewards investors
Partner is economic owner during the contract
Revenue sharing possible if returns are high
slides.narration: Let's look at the first type of DBFOM, the user-pays PPP, often called a concession. The authority gives the private partner the right to charge users, for example tolls on a road. The partner uses that money to pay its operating costs, repay its lenders and reward its investors. During the contract, the partner is the economic owner of the asset. It must maintain and renew it at its own cost and risk. And if traffic is much higher than expected, the contract may include revenue sharing, so the authority gets a share of the extra income.

slides.title: Filling the viability gap
points: Revenue too low to repay finance
Grants: co-financing
Performance-linked budget payments
Rail usually needs hybrid schemes
slides.narration: What if users cannot pay enough? The Guide calls this a viability gap. The project may still be very valuable to society, so the government can fill the gap. It can give grants towards construction, which we call co-financing. Or it can make extra budget payments that are linked to performance. Both are called viability gap funding. Roads, airports and ports often pay their own way. Rail almost never does, because it costs so much to build and fares are kept low. That is why rail projects often use hybrid schemes, mixing fares with availability payments.

slides.title: Government-pays: the PFI model
points: No users to charge, or free use intended
Paid for availability at agreed quality
Hospitals, prisons, schools, toll-free roads
Minority user revenue still allowed
slides.narration: The second type is the government-pays PPP, which the United Kingdom called PFI. Here the authority pays the partner from its budget. Why? Maybe there are no users to charge, like a prison. Maybe the revenue would be tiny compared with the cost. Or maybe the government wants the road to be free. The partner still finances, builds and maintains the asset. It is paid only as long as, and to the extent that, the asset is available at the agreed quality. It may earn some user revenue too, as long as that is not the majority.

slides.title: When the government keeps the tolls
points: I-595, Florida: tolled but government-pays
Partner receives availability payments
FDOT keeps tolls and traffic risk
Allows dynamic tolling to manage congestion
slides.narration: Here is a case that often confuses people. The I-595 road in Florida has tolls, yet it is a government-pays PPP. The private partner financed most of the project and receives availability payments once the road is open. The Florida Department of Transportation also paid large deferred grants. Crucially, the department keeps the toll money and the traffic risk. Why? It wanted freedom to change tolls to manage congestion. A private partner collecting tolls would want to maximise revenue instead. So always ask who receives the revenue, not just whether users pay.

slides.title: Joint ventures and institutional PPPs
points: JV: public equity, board votes, active management
Institutional PPP: government controls the company
True PPP only with significant private equity
Madrid Calle 30: 80% public, 20% private
slides.narration: Sometimes the government takes shares in the project company. If it has a material stake, votes on the board and helps manage the company, we call it a joint venture or mixed equity company. If the government actually controls the company, usually with most of the shares, it is an institutional PPP. The Guide accepts this as a true private finance PPP only when private investors hold significant equity, carry project risk, and the debt depends on performance. Madrid Calle 30 is an example, with the city holding eighty percent and a private partner twenty percent.

slides.title: Public-public partnerships are not PPPs
points: SOE owned by the procuring government
Often no contract in the strict sense
Reasonable doubt about real risk transfer
Guide focuses on conventional, privately controlled PPPs
slides.narration: Finally, the public-public partnership. Here a company wholly owned by the same government builds, finances and runs the asset. It may even use project finance and look very much like a PPP. But the Guide does not count it. Often there is no real contract, just a general authorisation. And even with a contract, there are reasonable doubts that any risk really leaves the public sector. So for the exam: one hundred percent public means not a PPP. The Guide's tender and contract guidance focuses on conventional PPPs, which are privately owned or controlled.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes a DBOM contract?
options: The contractor finances the works and is repaid from user charges
The contractor designs, builds, operates and maintains the asset, but the works are paid from the public budget
The contractor only builds the asset from a design prepared by the authority
The contractor designs and builds the asset and is repaid in fixed instalments after commissioning
quiz.explanation: In a DBOM the government pays for construction as work progresses and pays O&M in a separate stream. Repayment in fixed instalments after commissioning describes a DBF, not a DBOM.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements. 1: The PPP Guide regards DBOM as an infrastructure PPP. 2: The PPP Guide regards DBOM as a private finance PPP.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: DBOM is a type of infrastructure PPP but involves no private finance, so it is not a private finance PPP. Many countries also regard DBOM as a PPP.

quiz.question: When does a contract labelled DBFOM fail to be a true private finance PPP?
options: When the private partner creates an SPV to sign the contract
When the revenue comes from availability payments rather than users
When the investors take no material risk, so it behaves like a DBOM with private money
When the contract is for a hospital rather than a road
quiz.explanation: The Guide says a DBFOM is a true private finance PPP only with effective risk transfer and revenue linked to performance. Government-pays DBFOMs and social infrastructure can still be true PPPs.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT typical of a user-pays PPP (concession)?
options: The partner recovers its investment through charges paid by users
The partner maintains and renews the asset at its own expense and risk
The partner is the economic owner of the asset during the contract
The authority pays the partner fixed monthly availability payments as its main revenue
quiz.explanation: Availability payments as the main revenue are typical of government-pays PPPs. In a concession, all or most revenue comes from users.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: When a user-pays project's revenues cannot cover the partner's financial obligations and a return on equity, the Guide calls this a ____.
options: refinancing gain
viability gap
revenue sharing event
relief event
quiz.explanation: This shortfall is a financial or commercial viability gap. The government can fill it with grants (co-financing) or performance-linked budget payments.

quiz.question: In which sector does the Guide say user revenues will almost never cover the funding needs, so co-financing and hybrid payment regimes are standard?
options: Rail transportation
Airports
Ports
Toll roads
quiz.explanation: Rail combines very high capital needs with socially subsidised prices. The Guide names roads, airports and ports as sectors where user revenue is often enough.

quiz.question: In the I-595 project, users pay tolls. Why is it still classed as a government-pays PPP?
options: Because the private partner provided no finance
Because the tolls were paid directly to the construction contractor
Because the transport department kept the toll revenue and paid the partner availability payments
Because the contract was shorter than ten years
quiz.explanation: FDOT kept the tolls and the traffic risk and paid the partner availability payments, so the partner's revenue came from the government. The partner financed most of the project.

quiz.question: A city's wholly owned company signs a 25-year DBFOM-style agreement with the city, financed by a loan against its fare income. How does the PPP Guide classify this?
options: As an institutional PPP and a true private finance PPP
As a user-pays concession, because fares repay the loan
As a joint venture, because two public bodies are involved
As a public-public partnership, which is not a PPP
quiz.explanation: A 100% public company owned by the procuring government forms a public-public partnership, and there are reasonable doubts about real risk transfer. Using project finance does not change this.

quiz.question: Under the Guide, when may an institutional PPP be regarded as a true private finance PPP?
options: When the government holds 100% of the equity and appoints the board
When the private sector holds significant equity, assumes project risks and the debt is at risk of performance
When the project company is financed only with public grants
When the procuring authority also acts as the construction contractor
quiz.explanation: The Guide requires significant private equity, private assumption of project risks and management involvement, and debt at risk of performance. Full public ownership would make it a public-public partnership.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about Madrid Calle 30. 1: It was structured as a DBFOM with availability payments. 2: It was finally treated as on the municipal balance sheet, mainly because of insufficient risk transfer.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Madrid Calle 30 was a 35-year DBFOM with availability payments. Eurostat judged the risk transfer insufficient, so the project was recorded as public debt.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: If the contractor in a DBOM-type contract is not responsible for operating the infrastructure, the contract is usually called a ____.
options: DBM
DBF
DB
DBFM
quiz.explanation: Without operations, a DBOM is usually called a DBM (Ch 1 §2.2). DBFM is the name for a DBFOM without operations, so it includes private finance.

quiz.question: How is maintenance work usually paid for under a DBOM contract?
options: It is paid from user tolls that the contractor collects
It is paid on a cost-plus basis after each repair is done
It is financed by the contractor and repaid at hand-back
It is pre-contracted and paid by the government at a pre-agreed price
quiz.explanation: In a DBOM, maintenance is pre-contracted and paid directly by the government at a pre-agreed price (Ch 1 §2.2). The contractor does not finance anything and does not collect user charges.

quiz.question: Which risk usually remains mainly with the government in a DBOM contract?
options: Minor maintenance defects covered by liquidated damages
The contractor's own labour cost increases during works
Maintenance risk that depends on proper design and construction
Accidents on the construction site during the works
quiz.explanation: The Guide says the main part of maintenance risk, which depends on good design and construction, usually stays with the government. Only limited maintenance cost risk moves to the contractor, through liquidated damages.

quiz.question: Besides current operations and maintenance, what does the Guide say a DBFOM contractor is also responsible for?
options: Setting the user tariffs for the whole contract term
Managing the asset's life cycle, taking life-cycle cost risk
Regulating other operators in the same sector
Paying the authority an upfront fee for the asset
quiz.explanation: In a DBFOM the contractor finances the works and also manages the infrastructure life cycle, assuming life-cycle cost risks, usually through an SPV (Ch 1 §2.2). An upfront fee belongs to asset monetisation of existing assets, not to a new DBFOM.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about DBOM. 1: The contractor may still have an incentive to lower construction quality to save costs. 2: The contractor has capital at risk, which protects the authority against poor construction.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: The Guide warns that DBOM contractors may cut construction quality, so quality must be carefully controlled. There is no capital at risk in a DBOM, because the works are paid from the budget.

quiz.question: A ministry wants one firm to build and then run a small water plant, but the project and financial context do not justify a private finance PPP. Which option best fits the Guide's reasoning?
options: A DBOM, if the gain from integrated management is judged to exceed the loss
A DBFOM, because bundling build and O&M always needs private finance
A DB contract, then a cost-plus O&M contract with the same firm
A public domain concession granting the plant land for 99 years
quiz.explanation: The Guide says a government may choose DBOM when the benefit of integrated management exceeds the efficiency lost by not tendering O&M separately, often when a private finance PPP is not justified. Bundling does not require private finance.

quiz.question: What efficiency does a government give up when it chooses a DBOM instead of separate construction and O&M contracts?
options: The ability to pay for construction from its own budget
The chance to run a separate competition for the O&M contract
The right to set performance standards for maintenance
The option to keep legal ownership of the finished asset
quiz.explanation: The Guide says the loss of efficiency in a DBOM comes from giving up a separate competition for the future O&M contract. The government still pays from its budget and keeps ownership.

quiz.question: Which statement about DBOM and DBFOM-type contracts is correct according to the Guide?
options: They are usually the only forms that bundle long-term maintenance with construction
They are the only forms of infrastructure contract that include private finance
Neither of them links the contractor's pay to the performance of the asset
Both of them transfer the full life-cycle risk of the asset to the lenders
quiz.explanation: Only DBOM and DBFOM-type contracts (such as BOT) bundle long-term maintenance with construction, and they are usually the only forms paid on asset performance (Box 1.11). DBF also has private finance, and DBOM has none.

quiz.question: Which best describes how a DBFOM contract is financed?
options: The government pays for the works as they progress, and the contractor provides O&M
The contractor finances construction and is repaid in full when the works are complete
Lenders lend directly to the authority, which then pays the contractor for the works
The contractor provides all or most of the finance, from equity and lenders, at its own risk
quiz.explanation: In a DBFOM the contractor develops the asset with its own funds and funds from lenders, at its own risk (Ch 1 §2.2). Payment as works progress describes a DBOM, and full repayment at completion is closer to a DBF.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: A DBFOM-type contract that does not include operations in its scope is often called a ____.
options: DBM
DBOM
DBFM
BOO
quiz.explanation: The Guide says the contract is often called a DBFM when operations are not included. DBM is a DBOM without operations, so it has no private finance.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: The European Commission uses the term ____ for PPP structures in which a public body and private investors share the equity of the project company.
options: public-public partnerships
institutionalized PPPs
hybrid PPPs
regulated utilities
quiz.explanation: Box 1.7 says such structures are called mixed equity companies or joint ventures in some countries, and the EU Commission uses the term institutionalized PPPs. Hybrid PPPs are about mixing public finance or payments, not shared equity.

quiz.question: According to the Guide, which contract type, in terms of scope, is the only one that meets all the conditions of a private finance PPP?
options: DBOM, when maintenance risk is also transferred
DBF, when repayment follows commissioning
DBFOM and equivalents such as BOT or DBFM
Long-term management contracts with KPI deductions
quiz.explanation: The Guide says DBFOM (and DBFM, BOT, BOOT, BTO and so on) are the only contract type in terms of scope that fulfils all the conditions of a private finance PPP (Ch 1 §2.2). A DBOM has no private finance, and a DBF has no bundled O&M.

quiz.question: What makes a user-pays PPP different from a government simply earmarking toll revenue to its own highway enterprise?
options: The toll revenue is paid into the government's general budget each year
Future revenues are assigned by contract to a private partner's SPV to fund the asset
The toll revenue is used to fund the whole transport sector of the country
The government's own enterprise keeps the toll revenue and runs the road
quiz.explanation: The Guide defines a user-pays PPP as a contractual assignment to a private party of future revenues from public use of the asset. Paying tolls into the budget, a sector fund or a public enterprise are other uses of user revenue, not PPPs.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: User-pays PPPs are also known as ____, especially in civil code countries.
options: concession schemes
PFI schemes
affermage leases
institutional PPPs
quiz.explanation: The Guide says user-pays PPPs are also known as concession schemes, especially in civil code countries. PFI is the UK name for government-pays PPPs.

quiz.question: How is the financing of a user-pays DBFOM typically treated under national accounting standards, according to the Guide?
options: As public debt of the authority
As a capital grant of the authority
As an operating lease of the authority
As private finance
quiz.explanation: The Guide says in a user-pays PPP the financing is private and typically considered private finance under national accounting standards. Recording as public debt happens when risk transfer is insufficient, as in Madrid Calle 30.

quiz.question: In a user-pays PPP, how does the private partner give returns to its investors?
options: Through availability payments from the authority's budget
Through a fixed fee that is set in the lenders' loan agreement
Through equity dividends and/or repayment of shareholder loans
Through selling the asset to the authority at hand-back
quiz.explanation: The partner uses user payments to repay debt and to pay investors through dividends or repayment of shareholder loans (Ch 1 §2.2). Availability payments belong to government-pays PPPs.

quiz.question: In year 18 of a 30-year toll bridge concession, the bridge deck needs a major renewal that was foreseeable. Under the normal user-pays model, who should pay for it?
options: The authority, because it is the legal owner
The users, through a special surcharge set by the partner
The lenders, from a reserve they must fund themselves
The private partner, at its own expense and risk
quiz.explanation: As economic owner during the contract, the concessionaire must maintain and renew the asset at its own expense and risk, with no claim on the public party except where the risk allocation says otherwise (Ch 1 §2.2).

quiz.question: Traffic on a toll road concession is 40% above forecast, and the partner's revenue is far above the level needed for a minimum return. Which contract feature does the Guide say may let the authority benefit?
options: Viability gap funding paid by the authority to the partner
Deductions from the partner's monthly availability payments
Revenue sharing, with a payment from the partner to the authority
A compensation event claimed by the authority from the partner
quiz.explanation: When revenues exceed what is needed for a minimum return, a user-pays PPP may include revenue sharing, paid by the private party to the authority (Ch 1 §2.2). Viability gap funding flows the other way.

quiz.question: In the Guide's basic scheme of a user-pays DBFOM, what does the authority give the private partner?
options: Monthly availability payments
The right to charge users
A construction loan agreement
Shares in the EPC contractor
quiz.explanation: In Figure 1.5 the authority grants the right to charge users, and the partner provides the bundled DBFOM service. Loans come from lenders, and availability payments belong to government-pays PPPs.

quiz.question: According to the Guide's basic user-pays DBFOM scheme, what happens to the asset at the end of the contract?
options: It is handed back to the authority
It is sold to the project lenders
It stays with the SPV permanently
It passes to the EPC contractor
quiz.explanation: The basic scheme shows hand-back of the asset to the authority. Permanent private ownership is a feature of privatisation, not of a PPP.

quiz.question: Which are the two forms of viability gap funding named by the Guide?
options: Revenue sharing and refinancing gains shared with the authority
Shareholder loans and bond issues arranged by the SPV itself
Tax rebates for users and yearly increases in the tariffs
Grants (co-financing) and complementary budget payments linked to performance
quiz.explanation: The Guide says a viability gap can be filled with public grants (co-financing) or with complementary budget payments linked to performance. Revenue sharing goes from the partner to the authority, so it does not fill a gap.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about co-financing. 1: A government may fill a viability gap if the project brings enough economic and social benefits. 2: Co-financing can only be used when a user-pays project is not financially viable.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: The government may fill the gap when the project is still valuable for society. But the Guide notes that co-financing may be used even when a user-pays project is self-viable, for other reasons (Box 1.7).

quiz.question: Which describes a hybrid payment regime, such as those that are standard in rail PPPs?
options: User charges mixed with availability or service payments
Public and private equity mixed in the project company
Construction and O&M mixed in a single contract
Bank loans mixed with bond finance in the SPV
quiz.explanation: Box 1.7 describes hybrid payment regimes as mixing user charges with availability or service payments. Mixing public and private equity is a joint venture, not a hybrid payment regime.

quiz.question: A tram's fares will cover its O&M but not its capital cost. The government gives a capital subsidy during construction to reduce what the SPV must finance. How does the Guide describe this approach?
options: A public-public partnership run by the tram company
A government-pays PFI with no user revenue at all
An asset monetisation of an existing tram line
A hybrid structure that uses a subsidy to buy down capital costs
quiz.explanation: Box 1.7 says hybrid PPP structures can use capital subsidies or viability gap financing to buy down capital costs and make the project viable. Fares still flow to the SPV, so it is not a pure government-pays scheme.

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the features the Guide uses to identify a joint venture or mixed equity company?
options: The government holds a material equity stake
It has board seats with voting rights in line with its shares
The government guarantees the SPV's senior debt
It takes an active part in management, such as naming senior staff
quiz.explanation: The Guide's JV features are a material public equity stake, board seats with matching voting rights, and active management (Box 1.7). A debt guarantee is not part of the definition.

quiz.question: A regional authority takes a 10% stake in a toll road SPV, with only the normal rights of a minority shareholder. How would the Guide usually describe this?
options: An institutional PPP under public control of the SPV
A conventional PPP with government equity, not normally a JV
A public-public partnership, which is not a PPP
A mixed equity company, since any public stake counts
quiz.explanation: A simple minority stake with normal shareholder rights is not customarily called a joint venture (Box 1.7). An institutional PPP needs public control, usually a majority of shares.

quiz.question: Which is NOT a reason the Guide gives for choosing a government-pays PPP rather than a user-pays PPP?
options: There are no final users who could be charged
Potential revenue is small compared with capital needs
User revenue is high enough to repay all the financing
The government wants the asset to be free for users
quiz.explanation: The Guide lists no users to charge, revenue too small compared with capital needs, and a policy of free use (such as non-toll roads). High user revenue would suit a user-pays concession instead.

quiz.question: In a government-pays PPP, when is the partner paid for construction and O&M?
options: In instalments as construction work progresses on site
Only while the asset is available at the required quality
In one lump sum when construction is complete
According to its actual costs plus an agreed margin
quiz.explanation: The Guide says the government-pays partner is paid for both construction and O&M only as long as, and to the extent that, the asset is available at the specified standards. Payment as work progresses describes conventional procurement or DBOM.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about government-pays PPPs. 1: The government is always the user of the asset. 2: A school or a prison can be procured as a government-pays PPP.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: In some government-pays PPPs the government is not the user, for example a toll-free road used by the public. Hospitals, prisons, courts and schools are the Guide's examples of assets used by government.

quiz.question: A government-pays hospital PPP also lets the SPV earn income from a car park and shops, about 15% of its total revenue. How should it be classified?
options: Still a government-pays PPP, as user revenue is not the majority
A user-pays concession, because some users pay charges
A hybrid user-pays PPP with viability gap funding
Not a PPP, because commercial revenue is mixed in
quiz.explanation: The Guide says government-pays PPPs may include user or commercial revenue; if it is not the majority, the contract is still government-pays. The classification follows where most revenue comes from.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about names. 1: PFI is the name introduced in the United Kingdom for government-pays PPPs. 2: Some countries, especially in Latin America, use the term PPP only for government-pays contracts and call user-pays projects concessions.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Both are true (Ch 1 §2.2, footnote 21). This is why the same contract can have different names in different countries.

quiz.question: In the I-595 project, what did FDOT's $685 million of deferred grants allow it to do?
options: Transfer the toll traffic risk to the private partner
Avoid making any availability payments during operation
Keep the private partner out of the project financing
Use part of its budget early and lower its yearly availability payments
quiz.explanation: Box 1.8 says FDOT used part of its budget allocation in the early years while having lower yearly availability payment commitments. The partner still financed most of the project, and FDOT kept the traffic risk.

quiz.question: Why did FDOT decide to keep the toll revenue in the I-595 project instead of giving it to the private partner?
options: Because the partner refused to take any financing risk
Because the tolls were too low to cover the O&M costs
To keep flexibility for dynamic tolling to manage congestion
Because the lenders did not accept any traffic forecast
quiz.explanation: FDOT used dynamic tolling to manage congestion. A partner paid by tolls would want to maximise revenue, which could conflict with that aim (Box 1.8).

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about the I-595 project. 1: The deferred grants had to be repaid by the private partner from toll revenue. 2: FDOT carried the traffic revenue risk.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: The grants were not reimbursable and were paid in seven payments. The toll revenues stayed the property of FDOT, and therefore at its risk (Box 1.8).

quiz.question: In the EBRD model for urban transport described by the Guide, which agreement does the authority sign with the EBRD?
options: A Power Purchase Agreement
A direct agreement for step-in
A public domain concession
A Municipal Support Agreement
quiz.explanation: The authority signs a public service contract with its own public operator and a Municipal Support Agreement (MSA) with the EBRD to reinforce its financial commitment. The Guide does not treat this public-public structure as a PPP.

quiz.question: Consider these two statements about state-owned enterprises. 1: Many arrangements between governments and SOEs have no contract in the strict sense, only a general authorisation. 2: If an SOE arrangement uses project finance, the Guide then regards it as a PPP.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: The Guide notes that many SOE arrangements are only a general authorisation. Even with a strict contract and project finance, there are reasonable doubts about real risk transfer, so they are not PPPs.

quiz.question: In Madrid Calle 30, how was the private partner selected, and what else did it do?
options: By direct award; it also built the tunnels under a DB contract
By public tender; it also held 80% of the project company equity
By public tender; it also ran O&M under a back-to-back subcontract
By the lenders; it also collected tolls directly from road users
quiz.explanation: The city council chose the private partner by public tender. It took 20% of the equity and delivered O&M under a back-to-back subcontract paid from part of the availability fees (Box 1.9).

quiz.question: In Madrid Calle 30, who contracted the civil works contractors for the tunnels and road upgrades?
options: The private partner, under its O&M subcontract
The mixed equity company, after a separate selection
The city council directly, under a DB contract
The lenders, as a condition of their loan
quiz.explanation: Box 1.9 notes that the civil works contractors were selected in a separate process and contracted directly by the mixed equity company, Madrid Calle 30.

quiz.question: What is the main focus of the PPP Guide's tender and contract management guidance?
options: Conventional PPPs that are privately owned or controlled
Institutional PPPs controlled by the procuring authority
User-pays concessions only, not government-pays PPPs
PPPs with no public shareholding of any size at all
quiz.explanation: The Guide focuses on conventional PPPs, privately owned or controlled, possibly with a minority public stake. Most of its content still applies to joint ventures.

quiz.question: The city council held 80% of the Madrid Calle 30 project company. In the Guide's terms, what type of PPP is this?
options: A public-public partnership with no private shareholder
A conventional PPP with a minority public stake
A DBOM, because the works were paid by the city
An institutional PPP, controlled by the public party
quiz.explanation: A joint venture where the government controls the SPV, usually with most of the shares, is an institutional PPP (Box 1.9). It had a 20% private partner, so it was not public-public, and it was a DBFOM, not a DBOM.
